sentences.text: Eremiasaurus was a relatively small mosasaur, with the most complete specimen measuring 4.5 meters in length and a skull spanning 63.5 centimeters.

This animal possessed a robust skull featuring pronounced heterodonty, a condition where teeth vary significantly in shape and size along the jaws, with front teeth being straight and conical while middle ones were blade-shaped with serrated edges.
It is distinguished by an unusually high number of pygal vertebrae, a trait shared only with the genus Plotosaurus among known mosasaurs.

Unlike the wider-than-tall humeri found in Mosasaurus and Plotosaurus, the humerus of Eremiasaurus is roughly equal in height and width, while its fibula is bell-shaped and its finger bones are elongated and spindle-like.
The name Eremiasaurus translates to 'desert lizard' in Greek, honoring the arid modern climate of Morocco where the fossils were unearthed.
Fossils of this creature appear to have retained a hyoid bone, a feature that is rarely preserved in mosasaur remains.
The species holds the record for having one of the highest counts of pygal vertebrae known in any mosasaur.
Initial discoveries consisted of teeth found in Morocco and were first described by Camille Arambourg in 1952.
The species Eremiasaurus heterodontus was formally established in 2012 by Aaron R. H. LeBlanc and colleagues based on two nearly complete skeletons designated as syntypes, recovered near Sidi Daoui.
Changes in body proportions, specifically an increased number of pygal vertebrae, indicate that Eremiasaurus was a high-speed pursuit predator capable of rapid swimming.
Despite its specialized dentition, scientists debate whether the specific arrangement of teeth allows for a clear determination of its exact prey.

Evidence from the Ouled Abdoun Basin suggests that highly differentiated dental anatomy among local mosasaurs facilitated niche partitioning to reduce competition, with some species crushing shellfish while others hunted larger prey.
The genus Eremiasaurus was created in 2012, with Eremiasaurus heterodontus serving as the type species.
Phylogenetic analysis places Eremiasaurus heterodontus as the sister taxon to the tribe Plotosaurini, a relationship supported by the presence of an internarial keel.

Smaller, slender teeth once assigned to a related group are now attributed to Eremiasaurus, while larger teeth likely belong to Thalassotitan, though the validity of the tribe Plotosaurini has been questioned since 1997.

This extinct mosasaurine lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago, in phosphate deposits along the southern margin of the Mediterranean Tethys ocean.
